front:
Confidentiality

What does it protect, and what is one control that enforces it?
back: Only authorized parties can read the information. Enforced by encryption and access control. First leg of the CIA triad.

src.title: NIST Glossary: confidentiality
src.q: Preserving authorized restrictions on information access and disclosure

front:
Integrity

What does it protect, and what is one control that enforces it?
back: Data is not altered or destroyed in an unauthorized way. Detected with hashing and digital signatures.

src.title: NIST Glossary: integrity
src.q: Guarding against improper information modification or destruction

front:
Availability

What does it protect, and what is one control that enforces it?
back: Authorized users can reach the information and systems when needed. Supported by redundancy, backups and DoS defenses.

src.title: NIST Glossary: availability
src.q: Ensuring timely and reliable access to and use of information

front:
Authentication

What question does it answer?
back: Are you who you claim to be? Verifies the identity of a user, process or device, usually before access is granted.

src.title: NIST Glossary: authentication
src.q: Verifying the identity of a user, process, or device

front:
Authorization

What question does it answer, and when does it happen relative to authentication?
back: What are you allowed to do? It grants or denies access privileges, and comes after authentication succeeds.

src.title: NIST Glossary: authorization
src.q: Access privileges granted to a user, program, or process

front:
Accounting

The third A in AAA. What does it record?
back: Who did what, and when: usage and activity records that support auditing and billing. AAA = authentication, authorization, accounting.

src.title: RFC 2903: Generic AAA Architecture
src.q: Authentication, Authorization, Accounting (AAA) architecture

front:
Non-repudiation

What does it prevent, and which technology usually provides it?
back: A signer cannot later deny having sent or approved something. Provided by digital signatures made with a private key only the signer holds.

src.title: NIST Glossary: non-repudiation
src.q: assurance of the integrity and origin of data

front:
Control category: Technical

Who carries it out? Name two examples.
back: Carried out by the system itself through hardware, software or firmware. Examples: firewalls, encryption, access control lists, antivirus.

src.title: NIST Glossary: technical controls
src.q: primarily implemented and executed by the information system

front:
Control category: Managerial

What does it focus on? Name two examples.
back: Manages risk and the security program itself. Examples: policies, risk assessments, security planning, vendor reviews.

src.title: NIST Glossary: management controls
src.q: focus on the management of risk and the management of information system security

front:
Control category: Operational

Who carries it out? Name two examples.
back: Carried out mainly by people rather than by systems. Examples: security awareness training, incident response procedures, change reviews.

src.title: NIST Glossary: operational controls
src.q: primarily are implemented and executed by people

front:
Control category: Physical

What does it protect, and what are two examples?
back: Protects tangible space and equipment: locks, fences, badge readers, guards. NIST PE-3 requires verifying authorization at entry points, controlling entry and exit, and keeping access logs.

src.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: PE-3 Physical Access Control
src.q: Enforce physical access authorizations at

front:
Control type: Preventive

When does it act?
back: Acts before an incident to stop it from happening. Examples: firewall rules, least privilege, locked doors.

src.title: Wikipedia: Security controls
src.q: Preventive controls are intended to prevent an incident from occurring

front:
Control type: Detective

When does it act?
back: Identifies and alerts on an event while or after it happens. Examples: log monitoring, IDS, motion sensors, audits.

src.title: Wikipedia: Security controls
src.q: Detective controls are intended to identify, characterize, and log an incident

front:
Control type: Corrective

When does it act?
back: Limits damage and restores normal operation after an incident. Examples: restoring from backup, patching, quarantining a host.

src.title: Wikipedia: Security controls
src.q: corrective controls are intended to restore damage caused by the incident

front:
Control type: Compensating

When do you use one?
back: A substitute used when the recommended control cannot be applied, and it must give comparable protection. Example: extra monitoring on a legacy system that cannot be patched.

src.title: NIST Glossary: compensating security control
src.q: employed by an organization in lieu of a recommended security control

front:
Zero trust

What is the core idea, and what does it replace?
back: No implicit trust from network location. Every request is evaluated for least-privilege access, per request. It replaces the trusted-inside, untrusted-outside perimeter model.

src.title: NIST SP 800-207, p.13
src.q: Zero trust (ZT) provides a collection of concepts and ideas designed to minimize uncertainty

front:
Zero trust: control plane vs data plane

What travels on each?
back: The zero trust components talk to each other on a separate control plane. The application data itself travels on the data plane.

src.title: NIST SP 800-207, p.18
src.q: components use a separate control plane to communicate

front:
Zero trust: Policy Engine (PE)

What is its job?
back: Makes the final decision to grant access to a resource for a given subject, using enterprise policy and other inputs. Works with the Policy Administrator.

src.title: NIST SP 800-207, p.18
src.q: This component is responsible for the ultimate decision to grant access to a resource

front:
Zero trust: Policy Administrator (PA)

What is its job?
back: Carries out the PE's decision by establishing or shutting down the communication path between subject and resource.

src.title: NIST SP 800-207, p.18
src.q: This component is responsible for establishing and/or shutting down the communication path

front:
Zero trust: Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)

What is its job?
back: The gate on the data path. Enables, monitors and terminates connections between a subject and a resource.

src.title: NIST SP 800-207, p.19
src.q: This system is responsible for enabling, monitoring, and eventually terminating connections

front:
Zero trust: implicit trust zone

What happens to it as zero trust is adopted?
back: The area where everything is trusted once past the entry point. Zero trust shrinks these zones as far as possible, making access rules granular.

src.title: NIST SP 800-207, p.13
src.q: shrinking implicit trust zones

front:
Physical access monitoring

Name three ways to detect physical security incidents.
back: Guards, video surveillance and physical access logs reviewed for anomalies. Results feed incident response.

src.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: PE-6 Monitoring Physical Access
src.q: Monitor physical access to the facility where the system resides

front:
Honeypot

What is it, and what is it used for?
back: A system or resource built to be attractive to attackers so their activity can be detected and studied. Variants: honeynet (a network of them), honeyfile (bait file), honeytoken (bait credential or record).

src.title: NIST Glossary: honeypot
src.q: designed to be attractive to potential crackers and intruders

front:
Deception and disruption

What three jobs do decoy components do?
back: Decoys such as honeypots and honeynets are targets built to detect, deflect and analyze malicious attacks.

src.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: SC-26 Decoys
src.q: Include components within organizational systems specifically designed to be the target of malicious attacks

front:
Change management: approval

Who decides, and what must they consider?
back: Proposed configuration-controlled changes are reviewed and approved or disapproved, with explicit security and privacy impact considered. Decisions are documented.

src.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: CM-3 Configuration Change Control
src.q: Review proposed configuration-controlled changes to the system and approve or disapprove such changes

front:
Change management: impact analysis

When is it done?
back: Before the change is implemented, analyze it for potential security and privacy impacts.

src.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: CM-4 Impact Analyses
src.q: Analyze changes to the system to determine potential security and privacy impacts

front:
Baseline configuration

How can one be changed?
back: A formally reviewed and agreed set of specifications at a point in time. It can only be changed through change control procedures.

src.title: NIST Glossary: baseline configuration
src.q: formally reviewed and agreed on at a given point in time

front:
Configuration (change) control

What does it protect against?
back: Controls modifications to hardware, firmware, software and documentation so the system is not improperly modified before, during or after implementation.

src.title: NIST Glossary: configuration control
src.q: Process of controlling modifications to hardware, firmware, software, and documentation

front:
Allow list vs deny list

What is an allow list, and how does a deny list differ?
back: An allow list is a documented list of elements permitted by policy, and everything else is blocked. A deny list is the inverse: only listed items are blocked.

src.title: NIST Glossary: allowlist
src.q: A documented list of specific elements that are allowed

front:
Encryption

What does it produce?
back: The cryptographic transformation of data into ciphertext, which only holders of the right key can reverse.

src.title: NIST Glossary: encryption
src.q: The cryptographic transformation of data to produce ciphertext

front:
Key length

What is it, and why does it matter?
back: The length of a key in bits (also called key size). Longer keys make brute force harder.

src.title: NIST Glossary: key length
src.q: The length of a key in bits

front:
Symmetric encryption

How many keys, and what is the main weakness?
back: One shared key does both encrypt and decrypt, so it is fast. The weakness is getting that key to the other party safely.

src.title: NIST Glossary: symmetric key
src.q: A cryptographic key that is used to perform both the cryptographic operation and its inverse

front:
AES

What type of algorithm is it?
back: The Advanced Encryption Standard: a symmetric block cipher that works on 128-bit blocks, with 128, 192 or 256-bit keys.

src.title: NIST FIPS 197 (updated)
src.q: Each of them transforms data in blocks of 128 bits

front:
Asymmetric encryption

How many keys, and what is it commonly used for?
back: Two mathematically linked keys: what one does, the other undoes. Slower than symmetric, so used for key exchange and signatures.

src.title: NIST Glossary: asymmetric cryptography
src.q: Cryptography that uses two separate keys to exchange data

front:
Public key

What can you do with it, and who may have it?
back: The public half of a key pair. Anyone may hold it. It encrypts data for the key owner or verifies their signatures.

src.title: NIST Glossary: public key
src.q: The public part of an asymmetric key pair

front:
Private key

What can you do with it, and who may have it?
back: The secret half of a key pair. Only the owner holds it. It decrypts data or creates digital signatures.

src.title: NIST Glossary: private key
src.q: The secret part of an asymmetric key pair

front:
Key exchange

What problem does it solve?
back: Lets two parties establish keys for secure communication over an open network without having shared a secret beforehand.

src.title: NIST Glossary: key exchange
src.q: Process of exchanging public keys

front:
Transport / communication encryption

Which protocol protects data in transit on the web?
back: TLS: a protocol giving privacy and data integrity between two communicating applications, built from a Record layer and a Handshake layer.

src.title: NIST Glossary: transport layer security
src.q: A security protocol providing privacy and data integrity between two communicating applications

front:
Data at rest

How is it protected, and what should never be encrypted this way?
back: Protect it with encryption (full-disk, volume, file, database or record level). Passwords should be hashed, not stored with reversible encryption.

src.title: OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet
src.q: implementing solutions to protect data at rest

front:
Hashing

Name its key properties.
back: A one-way function producing a fixed-length output from any input. Used to check integrity. A tiny input change gives a very different hash.

src.title: NIST Glossary: hash function
src.q: A function on bit strings in which the length of the output is fixed

front:
Salting

What is a salt and what attack does it blunt?
back: A unique random value added to each password before hashing, so an attacker must crack hashes one at a time and cannot reuse precomputed tables.

src.title: OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet
src.q: A salt is a unique, randomly generated string that is added to each password

front:
Key stretching

How does a work factor help?
back: Repeat the hash many times so each guess is costly for an attacker. The work factor is the iteration count. Examples: PBKDF2, bcrypt.

src.title: OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet
src.q: The work factor is the number of iterations of the hashing algorithm

front:
Digital signature

What three things does it provide?
back: Origin authentication, data integrity and signer non-repudiation. Created with the signer's private key and verified with their public key.

src.title: NIST Glossary: digital signature
src.q: provides a mechanism for verifying origin authentication, data integrity, and signatory non-repudiation

front:
Public key infrastructure (PKI)

What does it do?
back: The framework that issues, maintains and revokes public key certificates so keys can be tied to identities.

src.title: NIST Glossary: public key infrastructure
src.q: A framework that is established to issue, maintain and revoke public key certificates

front:
Certificate authority (CA)

What does it do?
back: A trusted entity that issues and revokes public key certificates, vouching for who owns the key.

src.title: NIST Glossary: certificate authority
src.q: A trusted entity that issues and revokes public key certificates

front:
Root of trust: root CA and trust anchor

Why are they special?
back: The root CA's public key is the most trusted starting point of every trust path. A trust anchor is that base of the chain, pre-installed in devices and browsers.

src.title: NIST Glossary: root certificate authority
src.q: the certification authority (CA) whose public key serves as the most trusted datum

front:
Certificate signing request (CSR)

What does it contain, and who receives it?
back: Sent to a CA to apply for a certificate. Contains the requester's public key and identity details, and is signed with the matching private key.

src.title: NIST Glossary: certificate signing request
src.q: A request sent from a certificate requester to a certificate authority

front:
Self-signed certificate

Who signs it, and why is it not trusted by default?
back: Signed with the private key of its own subject, so no third-party CA vouches for it. Fine for lab use, but clients will not trust it by default.

src.title: RFC 5280 (X.509 PKI profile)
src.q: The signature on a self-signed certificate is generated with the private key associated with the certificate

front:
Wildcard certificate

What does it cover, and what is the risk?
back: Names like *.example.com cover many hosts under one certificate. If its private key leaks, every covered host is exposed.

src.title: RFC 6125: Service Identity
src.q: contains the wildcard character '*' as part or all of a label

front:
Certificate revocation list (CRL)

What is it, and what is its weakness?
back: A list of revoked certificates, signed by the CA. Clients must download and check it, so it can be large and out of date.

src.title: NIST Glossary: certificate revocation list
src.q: A list of revoked public key certificates created and digitally signed by a certification authority

front:
OCSP

How does it differ from a CRL?
back: An online protocol that asks a responder for the status of one certificate in real time, instead of downloading a whole list.

src.title: NIST Glossary: OCSP
src.q: An online protocol used to determine the status of a public key certificate

front:
Key escrow

Why would an organization keep copies of keys, and what is the risk?
back: Retaining the private component of an encryption key pair so data can be recovered if the owner loses it. The escrow store becomes a high-value target.

src.title: NIST Glossary: key escrow
src.q: The retention of the private component of the key pair associated with a subscriber

front:
Key management system

What part of a key's life does it handle?
back: Manages keys and their metadata across the lifecycle: generation, distribution, storage, backup, recovery, use, revocation and destruction.

src.title: NIST Glossary: key management system
src.q: A system for the management of cryptographic keys and their metadata

front:
Trusted Platform Module (TPM)

What is it and what does it protect?
back: A tamper-resistant chip on the motherboard that performs cryptographic operations, including key generation, and protects keys and small secrets.

src.title: NIST Glossary: trusted platform module
src.q: A tamper-resistant integrated circuit built into some computer motherboards

front:
Hardware security module (HSM)

Why use one instead of storing keys in software?
back: Dedicated hardware (or a virtual equivalent) that stores and uses keys, greatly lowering the risk of key extraction from memory.

src.title: OWASP Key Management Cheat Sheet
src.q: Hardware Security Module (HSM) or Trusted Platform Module (TPM)

front:
Steganography

What does it hide, compared with encryption?
back: Hides the very existence of a message, for example inside an image. Encryption hides the content but not the fact that a message exists.

src.title: NIST Glossary: steganography
src.q: communicating in a way that hides the existence of the communication

front:
Data masking

What does it do to a value?
back: Removes or replaces a field, for example with asterisks or a pseudonym, in a way that does not preserve the analytic value.

src.title: NIST Glossary: masking
src.q: The process of systematically removing a field or replacing it with a value

front:
Tokenization

What replaces the sensitive value, and how is it reversed?
back: Swaps sensitive data (like a card number) for a surrogate token. De-tokenization redeems the token for the original through a protected vault.

src.title: PCI SSC: Tokenization Guidelines
src.q: Tokenization is a process by which the primary account number (PAN) is replaced with a surrogate value

front:
Blockchain

What makes it tamper evident?
back: A distributed ledger of signed transactions grouped in blocks. Each block is cryptographically linked to the previous one after consensus, so edits are detectable.

src.title: NIST Glossary: blockchain
src.q: A distributed digital ledger of cryptographically-signed transactions
